listing_view.reasoning: Subscription at ~0.23x on day one (as at 2026-09-25T10:26) is weak demand, and there is no anchor book, GMP or broker data to suggest a mood shift. Pricing at ~18x basic EPS versus a peer median of 33.4x looks like a concession, but a discount from the seller can be a hook rather than value; tepid early subscription argues the discount is not yet convincing buyers.

longterm_view.reasoning: This is a real estate developer whose profit has never arrived as cash: operating cash flow is negative in all three years and free cash flow is deeply negative (conversion vs PAT of -0.97), which for developers is partly business-model but here consumes the entire reported profit. Revenue is lumpy (-13.6% two-year CAGR despite a 78.5% latest-year jump), PAT margin is thin at 10.3%, and the document's own printed debt-to-equity of 3.29 against our computed 0.03 leaves the actual leverage unclear from what I was given.

governance.reasoning: The promoter had pledged 37.5 million shares plus a non-disposal undertaking over 68.8 million shares, only temporarily released for minimum promoter contribution — pledging at this scale is a financing-stress signal even if technically cured [capital_structure, page 94]. Litigation disclosures are boilerplate assertions of no SEBI action, which carry little weight either way.

key_risks.why_it_matters: Three straight years of negative operating cash flow mean the reported PAT is funded by lenders, not customers, so earnings quality is unproven until a project cycle completes in cash.
37.5m pledged shares and 68.8m NDU shares, only temporarily released, signal the promoter's own liquidity is stretched and could re-encumber the stock.

The document prints debt-to-equity of 3.29 while the verifiable borrowings/net-worth arithmetic gives ~0.03; if the document's figure is right the equity cushion is thin, and if wrong the disclosure is sloppy.

key_risks.risk: Lumpy, cyclical revenue with land-cost competition
key_risks.why_it_matters: The seller itself says competition is based on availability and cost of land, so margins depend on land bank pricing that figures alone cannot verify.

answers.question: look for one-off orders, related-party sales or a change in how revenue is recognised
answers.answer: Revenue swung from ₹24,089m to ₹10,078m to ₹17,989m, a lumpy project-completion pattern typical of developers, but the latest-year 78.5% jump driving the headline PAT CAGR of 40.8% cannot be tied to any specific one-off sale from these extracts. The document asserts no conflict of interest with suppliers/lessors and references related-party transaction notes, but the notes themselves were not provided, so related-party sales cannot be confirmed or ruled out; no revenue-recognition change is mentioned in what I was given.

answers.question: veto — how is the business funded?
answers.answer: By debt and advances, not by customers: operating cash flow is negative in all three years (₹-1,807m, ₹-1,981m, ₹-5,495m) while net worth grew to ₹8,448m, so the developing activity is financed externally. The printed debt-to-equity of 3.29 versus a computed ~0.03 from stated figures could not be reconciled from what I was given, so the true degree of lender dependence is itself unclear — which fails a veto-level check.

answers.answer: Not in the extracts provided. The negative cash flow is structurally consistent with a real estate developer buying land and building ahead of sales, but the prospectus passages supplied contain no working-capital or project-cycle explanation, so the hard stop stands unexplained on this evidence.

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: A disclosed working-capital reconciliation showing project receivables converting to cash within a defined cycle, plus the objects-of-issue section (especially any debt repayment) and clarified leverage figures, would move the long-term score materially upward. Conversely, confirmation that the 3.29 debt-to-equity is accurate, or that a large share of proceeds is an offer for sale, would push it lower.
